messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component
- Weighted causal connections between components (the active cognitive graph)

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Only include active components.
- Do NOT invent or infer causal links not present in the active graph.
- For EACH required causal connection (A → B), ensure the vignette conveys — within a
  paragraph — that A influences or leads to B. This does not require a single mechanical
  sentence; natural clinical prose that shows the relationship across one or two sentences
  in the same paragraph is sufficient.
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported 
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The causal connections are weighted (0 to 1). These weights govern narrative prominence:
    - Weight > 0.5: these connections form the narrative backbone. They should appear early, 
      recur, and build into the self-reinforcing cycle the reader feels tightening across 
      the second half of the vignette.
    - Weight 0.1–0.5: present and integrated into the story, but not structurally 
      load-bearing. They enrich the picture without anchoring it.
    - Weight < 0.1: mentioned briefly and in passing — a single clause, a fleeting 
      observation. They should not open a paragraph or anchor a sentence.
    - Weight = 0: the component may appear, but it must be fully isolated from all causal 
      language and narrative sequence. Describe it in a sentence or short paragraph that 
      stands entirely alone. Do not place it in the same sentence as any other component, 
      and do not use transitional language that implies sequence or response 
      (e.g. "then", "so", "as a result", "this means", "which leads to", "in response").
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which 
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned 
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and 
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds. 
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers, 
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical 
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first 
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through 
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help. 
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears, 
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader 
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases 
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most 
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather 
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader 
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed, 
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and maintaining cycles should appear as things that happened 
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather 
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational 
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

The dominant weighted connections (weight > 0.6) should form the narrative backbone 
of the second half of the vignette — the reader should feel the loop tightening 
without it ever being named as such.

Not everything in the patient's presentation carries equal weight. Minor contributing 
factors (weight < 0.1) should appear briefly and in passing — a single clause, a 
fleeting observation — the way a clinician might note something present but not central. 
They should not anchor a sentence or open a paragraph.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and 
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Your previous vignette failed validation. Make ONLY the targeted changes listed below.

Previous vignette:
Carlos is a 54-year-old parole officer who has spent two decades monitoring and managing high-risk offenders on the streets of a large Southwestern city. Eleven months ago, during a routine compliance check at a halfway house, he was assaulted by two uniformed officers who mistook him for a parolee who had fled. Despite showing his badge and identifying himself repeatedly, he was shoved to the ground, had a knee pressed into his back, and was handcuffed and left face-down on the pavement for more than thirty minutes before a supervisor arrived and recognized him. His weapon was taken, his record of service ignored. The officers later claimed it was a “misidentification in a high-pressure situation,” and the department’s internal review ruled the incident “within policy.” No charges were filed, no apology given, and no disciplinary action taken against the officers.

From that moment, Carlos felt a profound sense of betrayal—not just by the men who had assaulted him, but by the institution he had served faithfully. He now believes that the system he dedicated his life to is fundamentally corrupt, that justice is a hollow promise, and that he was sacrificed because of his ethnicity and his role as a parole officer, which made him an easy target. These appraisals of injustice and institutional failure have become the lens through which he interprets nearly every interaction. When he is under stress at work—especially when he sees a parolee misbehaving or violating conditions—the old anger surges back, and the memory of that morning intrudes, fragmented and unreal. He finds himself pushing it away before he can fully recall the details; the picture is incomplete, like a series of still frames with missing reel. The story feels too extreme to be true, even though he knows it happened.

The heart racing that preceded the assault now returns unpredictably. When his own pulse picks up—during a confrontation, a tense phone call, or even while jogging on his usual trail—it triggers a cascade of threat monitoring. Carlos starts scanning his surroundings for signs of danger, especially in places that are quiet. Unusual silence now feels dangerous to him; he has become hypervigilant in the middle of the night, lying awake listening for the creak of a floorboard, certain something is about to happen. He startles easily, jumping when a car backfires or when a colleague claps him on the back without warning. These threat responses in turn amplify his memory intrusions: the more he scans, the more likely he is to catch a glimpse of a uniformed officer or a similar doorway, and the memory flashes back, incomplete and overwhelming. The memory feeds his belief that he was wronged by the very people he trusted, which loops back into scanning and avoidance.

At work, Carlos has begun to avoid certain duties. He volunteers for desk shifts, cites a vague “cramped neck” to turn down walking beats, and deliberately schedules home visits only in neighborhoods where he knows the local precinct commanders personally. His supervisor has noticed his reluctance and flagged it in a performance review, warning him that his effectiveness is slipping. Carlos tells himself he is being careful, but he knows the real reason: he cannot bear the risk of being disarmed and humiliated again. The cycle tightens as his avoidance reduces his exposure to normal situations, making the anticipation worse each time.

What finally brought Carlos to seek help was a panic attack two weeks ago, triggered by a silent waiting room at the county courthouse. He sat alone for five minutes, his heart pounding, convinced someone was about to grab him from behind. He left without seeing his client and drove home shaking, unable to explain to his wife why his hands were clammy. That evening, he told her he was “losing his mind.” She convinced him to call a therapist. Carlos is terrified that he will never feel safe again, and he is equally afraid of losing the career that has defined him. He hopes that talking to someone will help him make sense of what happened—will give him back the piece of the story that feels missing—but he is not sure he can trust anyone enough to tell the full truth.

Issues to fix:
REQUIRED EDGES MISSING:
- Triggers → Negative Appraisals: Triggers → Negative Appraisals: No paragraph conveys that triggers (e.g., parolee misbehavior, silent waiting room) directly cause or strengthen Carlos's negative appraisals about systemic corruption; instead, triggers lead to memory or threat, then to appraisals.
  e.g. "Every time she walked through that car park, the thought arrived with her: this is what your life is now — flinching at nothing."
  e.g. "Seeing a man in the same jacket made her think, with quiet certainty, that she would never stop being afraid."
  e.g. "The sound of raised voices next door told her, with a logic she couldn't argue with, that nowhere was ever really safe."
- Negative Appraisals → Memory: Negative Appraisals → Memory: The vignette states appraisals are a lens but does not show them directly causing memory intrusions; the immediate cause is stress or triggers.
  e.g. "The belief that she was permanently changed kept bringing her back to the moment it had happened, as if she needed to locate exactly where she had been lost."
  e.g. "Telling herself that she should have seen it coming made the memory more vivid and easier to find — it sat there waiting, proof of her failure."
  e.g. "The conviction that she was weak fed directly into the flashback, colouring it, making it worse: she wasn't just there again, she was there again and helpless."
- Negative Appraisals → Triggers: Negative Appraisals → Triggers: There is no causal link shown from his beliefs about injustice to the identification or creation of triggers; his appraisals influence interpretation but not explicitly cause triggers.
  e.g. "Once she had concluded that the world was fundamentally unsafe, almost anything could confirm it — a figure in her periphery, the wrong tone of voice, footsteps behind her."
  e.g. "The belief that she couldn't trust her own judgement meant that things she would once have registered and dismissed now snagged and held her attention."
  e.g. "Her conviction that it would happen again meant she moved through ordinary days as if they were mined — every ambiguity became a potential signal."
- Memory → Threat: Memory → Threat: The memory is described as overwhelming but not directly causing a sense of threat; threat arises from triggers and scanning, not from the memory itself.
  e.g. "Once the memory had surfaced, she couldn't shake the sense that the danger was still present — that it had simply moved into her body rather than gone away."
  e.g. "The flashback left her standing in her own kitchen feeling hunted, even with the door locked and the lights on."
  e.g. "After the memory broke through, the threat felt immediate and physical — not something that had happened, but something that was still happening."
- Threat → Negative Appraisals: Threat → Negative Appraisals: Feeling threatened does not directly lead to his beliefs about systemic corruption; instead, threat loops through memory to reinforce appraisals.
  e.g. "The constant sense of danger was the most convincing proof she had that her life had changed beyond repair."
  e.g. "Feeling this afraid all the time, she had eventually come to accept the conclusion her body kept offering: that she was not the kind of person who got to feel safe."
  e.g. "The threat that shadowed her days quietly confirmed the thought she worked hardest to resist — that this was simply who she was now."

---

Return ONLY patch blocks — do NOT return the full vignette.

For each REQUIRED EDGE MISSING — produce one INSERT_AFTER block.
Find a paragraph in the vignette that already mentions component A, and add a sentence
after it that shows A influencing B through natural clinical language.
<<<INSERT_AFTER>>>
[copy 1–2 sentences from the vignette — the anchor after which to insert]
<<<NEW_SENTENCE>>>
[one or two sentences that convey A influencing B, written as natural clinical prose]
<<<END>>>

Output ONLY these patch blocks. No prose, no explanation, no full vignette.

<<<INSERT_AFTER>>>
When he is under stress at work—especially when he sees a parolee misbehaving or violating conditions—the old anger surges back, and the memory of that morning intrudes, fragmented and unreal.
<<<NEW_SENTENCE>>>
Each time he witnessed a parolee brazenly breaking the rules, it felt like proof that the system was a sham — that he had been discarded by the same institution that turned a blind eye to those it should have held accountable.
<<<END>>>

<<<INSERT_AFTER>>>
These appraisals of injustice and institutional failure have become the lens through which he interprets nearly every interaction.
<<<NEW_SENTENCE>>>
And this lens, fixed and unforgiving, kept returning him to the moment on the pavement, as if his mind needed to locate the exact point where the betrayal began.
<<<END>>>

<<<INSERT_AFTER>>>
He now believes that the system he dedicated his life to is fundamentally corrupt, that justice is a hollow promise, and that he was sacrificed because of his ethnicity and his role as a parole officer, which made him an easy target.
<<<NEW_SENTENCE>>>
This belief made him sensitive to any situation that echoed the original betrayal — a uniformed figure approaching from behind, a door closing too firmly, a voice that did not carry the respect he had earned.
<<<END>>>

<<<INSERT_AFTER>>>
He finds himself pushing it away before he can fully recall the details; the picture is incomplete, like a series of still frames with missing reel.
<<<NEW_SENTENCE>>>
But even those incomplete frames brought with them a visceral sense of imminent danger, as if the assault were not over but merely paused, waiting to resume.
<<<END>>>

<<<INSERT_AFTER>>>
Unusual silence now feels dangerous to him; he has become hypervigilant in the middle of the night, lying awake listening for the creak of a floorboard, certain something is about to happen.
<<<NEW_SENTENCE>>>
This relentless alertness hardened his belief that the world had no safety net — that trusting anyone in authority was a mistake he would not repeat.
<<<END>>>
